title: I Found a 10-Second Time Machine ⏪ (Animated Short Film)
description:
It looked like a broken pocket radio from the nineteen-eighties, sitting abandoned on an empty subway bench. It had a single brass toggle switch and a glowing red button labeled: REWIND. When Pip accidentally knocked his scalding hot coffee off the bench, he slammed the red button in pure panic. A high-pitched metallic click rang out. Reality shivered. The coffee cup flew straight upward off the concrete, the spilling liquid sucked itself back into the mug, and the clock on the subway wall spun backward by exactly ten seconds.

With unlimited ten-second undos, Pip became completely invincible. In job interviews, if he said something awkward, click—he rephrased it with genius wit. At roulette tables, if the ball landed on black, click—he switched all his chips to red. He dodged speeding taxis, caught falling flower pots before they hit pedestrians, and never made another mistake. Pip was living life in god mode.

By day fourteen, Pip had clicked the rewind button over eight hundred times. But physics does not tolerate an eraser. Pip began noticing temporal ghosting—faint, translucent double-images of himself lagging two steps behind his body. Worse, every time he rewound reality, the rest of the world felt ten seconds colder, and people's conversations started skipping like scratched vinyl records.

Then came the incident at the downtown crosswalk. A runaway truck blew through a red light. Pip reached into his hoodie pocket and smashed the rewind button. The world shuddered backward—tires screeched in reverse, pedestrians drifted backward step-by-step. But as Pip turned around, his blood froze. Standing right in the center of the road was another stickman in a charcoal overcoat... looking directly into Pip's eyes, completely unaffected by the rewind.

👉 Option A: "KEEP THE REWIND REMOTE — Unlimited 10-second undos, but each click costs one month of your future lifespan."
👉 Option B: "DESTROY THE REMOTE FOREVER — Accept mistakes, heartbreak, and risk as proof of human free will."
